All rights regarding the publication, printing, and other matters concerning this work have been secured by the aforementioned eminent Mahārājas.
Oṃ namaḥ śivāya! Salutations to Śiva, whose form is consciousness, both sequential and non-sequential.
Now begins the *Kāmakalāvilāsa*, composed by the venerable Puṇyānandācārya.

I place within my heart that Blessed Lady who, through the interplay of resting upon the three steps, constantly shines forth loftily as she transcends those very three steps; she who, though her body is the single sequence, manifests as the very nature of non-sequentiality.
The supreme consciousness.

May Maheśa, whose body is pure light, protect us—he who is intent upon the playful diversion of the arising, abiding, and dissolution of the entire universe, and whose inner reflective awareness is ever-absorbed. (1)
In this context, because the *puṇyānandayogin* intends to expound the mantra-cycles of Tripurasundarī— who is the presiding deity of all sciences—
the two [deities] who constitute her substratum, namely Kāma and Kāmeśvarī, are [the subject].

First, they explain: "Sakaletyādi" means the arising (*udaya*)—that is, creation (*sarga*)—the maintenance (*sthiti*)—that is, protection (*rakṣā*)—and the dissolution (*laya*)—that is, destruction (*nāśa*)—of all worlds (*sakala-bhuvana*). This triad is indicative of restraint (*nirodha*) and grace (*anugraha*).
He is intent upon that diversion (*vinodana*), which is play (*krīḍana*), consisting of the sport (*līlā*) abundant with these fivefold functions.

The suffix *mayaṭ* here is prescribed in the sense of abundance (*prācurya*). This being the case, in response to the inquiry as to what the nature of Brahman is—whose characteristic is its transcendence of the world—it says: "with internalized reflection" (*antarlīnavimarśa*), and so forth. "Reflection" (*vimarśa*) refers to that which is reflected upon or perceived as "this," namely the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), in the form of "this."

The well-known reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the universe created by the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is of such a nature that its *vimarśa*—the manifestation—is internally dissolved or contained within it; thus, it is "one whose *vimarśa* is internally dissolved" (*antarlīnavimarśa*). This is the meaning here:
[He is] one who has assimilated the entire universe into His own self, and who is permeated by the contemplation of the perfect state of "I-ness" (*ahambhāva*); or else, [it means...]

Vimarśa is the innate self-awareness (*aham-parāmarśa*) which is the cause of the origin, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe. Accordingly, the *Nāgānanda* states: "Vimarśa is that which [manifests] through the form of the universe, the manifestation of the universe, or the withdrawal of the universe."
The uncreated manifestation of the universe as "I" has what is called its "internal absorption," which is inward-turnedness (*antarmukhatva*).

And thus, the meaning is this: that Supreme Lord, the Supreme Brahman, whose reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)—which is inward-turned and absorbed within—is the full sense of "I-ness" (*pūrṇāhaṃbhāva*), possesses the nature of light alone.
And he states its supremacy over all by saying, "whose body is pure light" (*prakāśamātratanuḥ*). Here,

what is called "lightness" (*prakāśatva*) is precisely the reflective awareness of "I" (*ahaṃparāmarśa*), which consists of the vibration inherent within the supreme person (*uttamapuruṣa*) in the form of "I desire," "I know," and "I act."
[Objection: But surely luminosity is also observed in the sun and other such things; how then can this [luminosity] alone belong to the Supreme Self? [Reply:
Because its essential nature is unconditioned by space, time, and form, and because it possesses lordship, that is, the quality of being the controller of all. || 1 ||
Even in the *Parābhaṭṭārikā*, he speaks of her being endowed with all forms:
"Victorious is that primordial Power (*śakti*), whose nature is eternally incomparable and consisting of innate bliss;
she is the seed of all future moving and unmoving beings, and a stainless mirror for the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the form of Śiva. (2)

That primordial, undivided power, the Supreme Goddess (Parābhaṭṭārikā), Mahātripurasundarī, is victorious; she exists in a state of supreme excellence. She is designated as Tripurā, renowned in all the Upaniṣads, as she consists of the thirty-six principles beginning with Śiva and ending with Earth, is the self of the entire phenomenal world, and yet transcends it.

Because she existed prior to the three fires (*tejas*), she is called Tripurā; and her preeminence over all is proclaimed everywhere in the *Āgamas*. This very point is elucidated by the passage beginning with "nijā" (intrinsic):
her form is intrinsic (*nija*), natural, consisting of bliss, unmixed with suffering, eternal (*nitya*)—meaning existing at all times—and incomparable and limitless.

Her own essential nature is such that she is the seed—the source, the cause—of the future moving and non-moving worlds, meaning the stationary and the animate that are yet to come into being. Now, one might object: just as Śiva’s status as the creator of the universe is not possible without Śakti...
This is indeed consistent; for even the supreme power (*parāśakti*) cannot possess causality without Paramaśiva.
Thus, how can it be said that she is "the seed of all future moving and non-moving beings"? To this, he says:
"She is the stainless mirror of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of Śiva’s own nature. This means that the nature (*svarūpa*) of Śiva is of the form "I" (*aham*). Of that [nature]...

"Vimarśa" is reflective awareness, a cognition of the nature "I am"; in its manifestation, it is like a stainless mirror, meaning it is skillful in perfect illumination. Just as a certain exceedingly beautiful king, having clearly beheld his own reflection in the surface of a clear mirror situated directly before him...
Just as one recognizes that reflection as "I," so too the Supreme Lord, having correctly beheld His own power which is under His control, realizes His own true nature. || 2 ||
Some say that Brahman is precisely the reflective awareness "I am full. How, then, is it said that Brahman possesses reflective awareness? To this, he says:
the Supreme Power (Parā-Śakti) takes the form of the sprout from the seed of the manifest union of Śiva and Śakti.
She shines, her form characterized by the script of unsurpassed contemplation upon the supreme form. || 3 ||
Here, by the word "Supreme" (parā), the aforementioned Mahātripurasundarī is designated;
she is described thus because she is well-known in the scriptures as being of the nature of consciousness, bliss, will, knowledge, and action.
She is said to be "having the form of the sprout from the seed of the manifest union of Śiva and Śakti"; for Śiva and Śakti together constitute "Śiva-Śakti."
The meeting (*samāgama*) of these two is their union (*saṃyoga*), which is manifest (*sphuṭa*) and evident. This is the union of Śiva and Śakti;

by means of this, [the universe]—consisting of seed and sprout—is produced. Just as there is a sprout from a seed and a seed from a sprout, the web of principles (*tattvajāla*), beginning with the principle of Śiva and ending with the principle of Earth, is manifested in successive stages. This is the meaning here.
By the word *śiva*, the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) is denoted, because the *śivatattva* is the substratum of the power of knowledge;
and by the word *śakti*, the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) is also denoted, because the *śaktitattva* is the substratum of the power of action.
This is because it is observed that the manifestation everywhere of that [reality] whose nature is consciousness and bliss occurs precisely through knowledge and action.
He further qualifies that very [deity]: "She shines, her form being characterized by the letters of the supreme *vimarśa* which are of the subtlest nature.
That which has a subtlest (*aṇutaratama*)—that is, an extremely minute—form is thus described; the letter 'A' is the supreme letter (*anuttara-lipi*), and the letter 'Ha' is the letter of *vimarśa*.
She whose form, that is, whose essential nature, is indicated by those two, is so called. Herein...

By the phrase "having as its objective form the letters of supreme reflective awareness," it is meant that the Supreme Power (Parā Śakti), whose nature is the "I" (Ahaṃ) and which contains within its womb the entire collection of phonemes, consists of the fifty letters beginning with 'A' and ending with 'Ha'.

It is stated that the Supreme Goddess (Parābhaṭṭārikā), the progenitress of the entire phenomenal world consisting of phonemes, words, mantras, kalās, principles (tattvas), and worlds, is the inner self of all beings;
she is perceived everywhere in the Vedāntas in the form "I, I. || 3 ||

From this point forward, the author proceeds with a detailed exposition to describe the primary subject—the *Kāmakalā* in the form of syllables—beginning with the words "The rays of the sun of Paraśiva" and ending with "the two *bindus*, whose forms are fire and the moon. As for Kāma, he is Śiva; [the author now describes] that which has the form of his syllable.
When the multitude of rays from the Sun of Supreme Śiva reflects in the pure mirror of self-awareness (vimarśa),
the Great Bindu settles upon the wall of consciousness, which is as radiant and beautiful as a gem.

Paraśiva, whose sole nature is light, is indeed the venerable Paramaśiva; he is the sun, the maker of day. His rays are its beams, and their mass is a cluster. Within that pure and stainless mirror of *vimarśa*—wherein *vimarśa* is a single, boundless power of vibration, as stated in the *Mālinīvijayottara-tantra*—[it resides].
That vibration (*sphurattā*) ...

by such [statements] is defined as being like a mirror, because it is the manifestation of its own essential nature (*svarūpa*). In that context, "reflection" (*pratiphalana*) means the beholding of one's own nature; when there is such beholding in the form of reflection, within that which consists of consciousness (*cittamaya*), [the Self is perceived].

Upon the wall whose sole nature is consciousness (*jñāna*), which is exceedingly beautiful and charming due to its constant self-luminosity, the Great Bindu (*mahābindu*) enters and becomes firmly established. The mind is described as a "wall" because it is the cause for the manifestation of the Great Bindu;
even in the world, after the reflection of the sun's rays occurs upon the surface of a mirror placed facing the sun—
Just as a point of light from the sun’s rays striking a nearby wall is perceived directly, so too,
when a connection with the self-reflection of one's own nature occurs— like a mirror— the Supreme Lord, whose nature is light,
shines forth there in the form of the Great Bindu (mahābindu) as "I am full. This is the meaning.
"And when one perceives the radiance of one's own self through scripture, then the arising of the wheel occurs.
Thus it is said in the *Pratyabhijñā* as well.
"That throbbing is the Great Being...
and so forth. Even for a yogin of supreme bliss, such words regarding "how muchness" (*iyattā*) and the like are far removed; it is to be known through one's own direct experience (*svānubhūti*).
How indeed can that consciousness, which is the totality of such a radiance, be described?
And so forth. || 4 ||

Triumphant is that egoity (ahaṃkāra), composed of consciousness, which takes the form of the perfectly manifest syllable *A* and is the very essence of the "I-sense" arising from the vision of one's own such resplendent power;
it is the mass of the union of Śiva and Śakti, having swallowed the entire circle of the worlds. 5.

"Ahaṃkāra" refers to that reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) which manifests as "I, I"—the cause (*kāra*) of this very [awareness] being the manifestation of the experience of a distinct self-remembrance; such an *ahaṃkāra* triumphs, existing with supreme excellence.
For:
The resting of light within itself is indeed proclaimed as the state of "I-ness" (ahambhāva).

It consists of consciousness, has knowledge as its sole nature, and takes the form of the perfect fusion of the clearly manifest vowels 'a' and 'ha'. Since 'a' and 'ha' are thus 'ahau', they are exceedingly manifest and distinct, yet their forms arise from one another; where these two clearly manifest letters become merged into a single unity, that is this state.

He is the mass (piṇḍa) consisting of the union of Śiva and Śakti; for this very reason, he has swallowed the circle of the worlds—that is, he by whom the circle of the worlds, composed of the aggregate of the thirty-six principles (tattvas), has been placed within.
This meaning follows the logic of sensory withdrawal (pratyāhāra).

From the very form of the *ahaṃkāra*—which encapsulates the entire collection of phonemes (*varṇa*) within itself and consists of the union of light (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)—the expansion of the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*), comprising both word and meaning, comes into being. And so says the Śruti:
"One single phoneme, through its connection with manifold powers, sustains many phonemes whose meanings are inherent."
Thus [ends the fifth].
Regarding what was stated previously— that "the Great Bindu enters into that which consists of consciousness"—
he teaches the *kāmakalā* therein by means of defining the nature of the Bindu:
"The pair of white and red Bindus, representing the distinct withdrawal and expansion of Śiva and Śakti."
The cause of the creation of both word and meaning, wherein they are clearly interpenetrated with one another.
I am the *bindu*, whose nature is the *ahaṃkāra*; the Sun is this form of the equal fusion (*samarasa*) of the couple.
Kāma is so called because of his loveliness, and the *kalā* consists of the forms of Fire and Moon; these two *bindus* are the forms of Fire and Moon.

"White" means bright; "red" means crimson. The two dots (*bindu*) possess those respective forms. Therefore, it is that action in which Śiva and Śakti—being distinct yet intent on sporting with one another—are present. For this very reason, it is "contracting and expanding," meaning that in which the expansion consisting of world-creation contracts, becoming like a closed bud. [This refers to] speech.
All sounds, beginning with Parā and Paśyantī,

are the objects [of consciousness] consisting of the thirty-six principles (tattvas) from Śiva down to Earth; their "emanation" (sṛṣṭi) is the creation of the world consisting of the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan), and therein the cause is the clearly manifest mutual interpenetration.

One should contemplate that very divine couple—the forms of Kāma and Kāmeśvarī—consisting of a pair of white and red drops, which are mutually and reciprocally interpenetrated, internalized, yet clearly distinct; such is the connection with what precedes. In this regard, this is an extreme secret.
"He who is supreme is Maheśvara.

According to this scriptural teaching, the Supreme Lord— the ineffable source from which all words such as the Vedas arise— possesses the power of *vimarśa* (reflective awareness), which consists in the dissolution of the entire phenomenal universe that constitutes His own body.

Having entered into the state of the *bindu*, that power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*) likewise enters into the *bindu* consisting of light which is within itself; thereupon, the *bindu* comes into being.

From that *bindu* arises [the power] whose nature is resonance (*nāda*), which contains all the *tattvas* within it, which consists of splendor, and which is the form of the individual soul (*jīva*), like the tip of a hair.

By its subtle form, it assumes the shape of a *śṛṅgāṭaka* (triangular node). Thus, the body "I" (*ahaṃ*) arises from those two, light (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), whose natures are the *bindu* and *nāda*. In this way, between those two which possess two forms, one—reflective awareness—assumes the form of the red *bindu*, while the other is light.
Upon the union of the two, it attains the state of a white drop; through its mixed form, it becomes the nature of the Supreme Self, consisting of all splendor. As the Śruti also says:
"The one color [becomes manifold] through the application of power."
"It assumes many colors while maintaining its inherent purpose.
This explains the very definition of the three *bindus*; thus, "the *bindu* is the essence of the *ahaṃkāra*. The term *bindu* [is used here].

He whose self is of the nature of identity with that [Reality], whose own nature is identity, is the Self—the ego-consciousness (*ahaṃkāra*) which is white and red in form, which contains within itself the entire collection of phonemes (*varṇa-rāśi*), and which is the ego-consciousness in its expansive form as the Absolute (*anuttara*). By the rule "the suffix *kāra* is added after a phoneme," the suffix *kāra* is applied to the word *ahaṃ*, just as in the case of the vowel *ai*. For this very reason:
"Having the form of the union of this couple":
the couple (*mithuna*) is the pair (*dvandva*) consisting of these two—illumination (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), which are denoted by the letters *a* and *ha*;
the "union of flavors" (*samarasa*) is the harmony consisting of their mutual penetration; that very thing is the "form," meaning the essential nature (*svarūpa*), of [the deity].

He, being thus, is the Sun (Ravi) who has attained the state of essential identity with the white and red bindus; that is to say, he is the "mixed bindu" (miśrabindu). For in the world, the Sun possesses this mixed nature due to its identity with Agni and Soma; for this very reason, it is fit to be worshipped. He explains this by the word "Kāma":
it is called "Kāma" because it is desired and sought after as one's own Self by great yogis who perceive the ultimate reality. The reason for this is as follows:

"By way of desirability" means by means of the state of being desirable, that is, the state of being longed for. *Kalā* is the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*), *dahana* is fire, and *indu* is the moon; those two are the forms of which the two *bindus* consist—thus they are the "fire-moon-bodied *bindus*.
Herein the meaning is this: the power of reflective awareness has the nature of both fire and the moon.

Mahātripurasundarī, who is inseparable from Kāmeśvara—the embodiment of both [Śiva and Śakti]—is called the *Kāmakalā*, whose form is the totality of the *bindu*. She alone is proclaimed in all the Āgamas as the object of worship. And it has been said:
"She whose face is the sun and the *bindu*, and beneath whom shine the two breasts consisting of the moon and the fire-*bindu*..."
Worship eternally this supreme goddess, who is the locus for the creation of the digits of the latter half of the aeon.
The bindu situated above the letter *e* is the face;
the sun and moon, moving downward, are the two breasts; and the half-moon digit (*kalā*) is the womb.
Such is the secret. The essential point here is this:

she is known as Kāmakalā, whose nature is the Great "I-consciousness" (mahāhaṃtā) filled with the potency of the great mantra consisting of the infinite mass of phonemes within herself; whose essence is light and bliss; and who takes the form of the syllable *lipi*, which is the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) of the three *bindus*.
"Mahātripurasundarī, the Mātṛkā, is to be meditated upon incessantly by the supreme yogis, the great devotees of Maheśvara. Thus it is stated; and in the *Vijñānabhairava* as well:
"But [the worship] of the wheel in the form of the Bindu is performed according to the sequence of gross phonemes (*sthūlavarṇakrama*)."
Through the upward movement (uccāra) of the void that concludes with the half-moon, the bindu, and the nāda, one becomes Śiva.
Thus [ends the seventh section].
Having thus indicated the nature of the Bindu, he states that the fruit of the worship of knowledge is indeed the state of the Supreme Brahman:
"Thus is this Kāmakalā-vidyā, which consists of the sequence of the Devī-cakra."
By whomsoever she is known, he becomes liberated and takes on the form of Mahātripurasundarī. || 8 ||

The *Kāmakalā*, namely Mahātripurasundarī, has been explained by means of the great treatise mentioned previously. In response to the inquiry as to what kind of *vidyā*—that is, knowledge—she possesses, [the author] says: "The Goddess consists of the sequence of the *cakras*.
The *cakra* of the Goddess Tripurasundarī is the Śrīcakra; its "sequence" (*krama*) is that which is designated as consisting of the *cakras*, the mantras, and the deities.

That person who, through the descent of grace (*śaktipāta*), has known and realized— as one who meditates upon it— that [reality] which consists of all forms from *Sarvānandamaya* down to the most manifest (*prakaṭa*), and which has that as its essence and is the object thereof, becomes liberated.
He is indeed liberated, a mass of consciousness whose sovereignty is made manifest by knowledge and supernormal powers;

thus, according to the principle of *Pratyabhijñā*, the supreme yogi— who is adept at eradicating the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of transmigratory existence— continually dwells even at the end [of life] in the form of Mahātripurasundarī, possessing identity with the essence of the Supreme Goddess (Parābhaṭṭārikā).
It comes to be. || 8 ||
He begins to describe the origination of the world and so forth from the very point of the bindu, which is the ultimate reality and the primordial nature:
"From the throbbing, ruddy bindu, the sound of the sprout of Nāda-Brahman becomes manifest;
from that arises the manifestation of ether, air, fire, water, earth, and the [five] elements. (9)
From the throbbing, swelling *bindu* characterized as previously described, arises the sprout of *nāda-brahman*:
*nāda* is the phoneme that is the cause of the production of all sounds; it is itself *brahman*, and it is that whose sprout is this *brahman*.
Thus it has been said:
There is one phoneme whose essence is sound (nāda), which contains all divisions of sound;
because its nature never sets, it is known as the "unstruck" (anāhata).

Thus, the sound— which is of the nature of the Brahman of Sound (nādabrahman) in its suchness— manifests as the articulated speech beginning with Paśyantī; from that sound, the origin and production of the five elements (space, air, fire, water, and earth), as well as the phonemes from 'a' to 'kṣa', is traditionally taught.

Having thus described the state of being the self of all and the creator of all belonging to the red drop (śoṇabindu), he now extends that same nature here to the white drop (śubhrabindu) as well: "Now, from the white drop also arises the birth of ether, air, fire, water, and earth."
This entire world, from the atom up to the cosmic egg, is a transformation of these five elements.

The meaning is that from the "clear" (*viśada*), which is the previously explained "all-illuminating" (*sarvaprakāśa*) *bindu*, the infinite Brahmāṇḍas, consisting of the five elements beginning with space (*gagana*), undergo manifestation and dissolution. And so says the Āgama:
I bow to the great seat of consciousness, which is the supreme refuge of Śiva and Śakti, and which manifests as the infinite play of rays that constitute the world through its own spontaneous will.
Thus [ends the tenth].
Having thus explained the non-duality of the two drops (*bindu*), he states their identity with the mantra and the deity by means of that same analogy:

"Just as the two drops are devoid of mutual distinction, so too there is not even a trace of difference between the Vidyā and the deity, who are respectively the object of knowledge and the knower. (11)

Just as the two *bindus*, which consist of the previously mentioned light (*prakāśa*) and awareness (*vimarśa*), are devoid of differentiation in whatever manner they exist— this indeed the wise call the reality (*tattva*) known as Śiva-Śakti.

According to the principle thus stated, they are mutually embraced; in that very manner, there is not even a trace of difference—not even the slightest distinction—between the Vidyā and the Deity. Here, "Vidyā" refers to the fifteen-syllable mantra, and the "Deity" is Mahātripurasundarī. Between these two—the object of knowledge and the knower, the signified and the signifier—there is no disparity whatsoever. Thus, from this inseparable couple consisting of Nāda and the rest, the entire universe [emerges].
It manifests. || 11 ||
That very couple, by their own will, made their own distinction non-distinct; thus he says:

"Speech and meaning are eternally joined with one another, consisting of Śakti and Śiva. These two, divided into the distinctions of emission, maintenance, and withdrawal, exist in three ways through the form of the three seed-syllables. (12)
16) Speech consists of phonemes, words, and mantras; its meaning consists of the categories (kalā), principles (tattva), and worlds (bhuvana). Why does it have this form?
Precisely because of the word and its meaning, which consist of manifestation (prakāśa) and reflective awareness (vimarśa).

Because it is heard that the entire manifold of phenomenal existence (*prapañca*), consisting of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*), arises from this very source; therefore, [the relationship] is eternally joined and continuously conjoined. Indeed, there is no occasional connection as between a jar and a cloth; for if that were the case, the undesirable consequence would follow that everything could arise at any time.

Regarding the distinctions of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), maintenance (*sthiti*), and dissolution (*laya*): emanation is the manifestation of the network of principles (*tattva*) beginning with Śiva and ending with the earth. Maintenance is... [the preservation of that manifested order].
Their preservation is their dissolution; their being made one's own is the state of oneness. Such is the difference between those two.
Furthermore, the self-nature of these three is as follows, and thus Abhinavaguptapāda [states]:
"The processes of emanation and withdrawal reside within one's own self, established as one's essential nature."

Thus: the two, consisting of Śakti and Śiva and having the nature of Light (prakāśa) and Reflection (vimarśa), do not constitute separate principles because of their mutual identity, just as fire and its power to burn are not distinct. And there is a saying by the learned: "The identity of these two is eternal, like that of fire and its power to burn."

Thus: these two previously mentioned, light (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), exist in three ways—that is, they are divided and distinct. By what means? He says: "in the form of the three seed-syllables," meaning by way of being composed of the seed-syllables of Vāgbhava, Kāmarāja, and Śakti. This is the meaning.
Mahātripurasundarī, whose form consists of the syllable Kāmakalā which is the unified totality of the three drops, is the object of all worship.
From this point onward, he begins to extract the venerable fifteen-syllabled Vidyā by means of describing the specific objects contained within the three sections beginning with Vāgbhava:
"The Mother, the Measure, the Measured, and the three Bindus are the forms of the distinct seed-syllables."
And those which are conceived as being divided into the three abodes (dhāma), the three seats (pīṭha), and the three powers (śakti). || 13 ||
In them, respectively, are the three genders and likewise the triad of Mātṛkās.
Thus, the Vidyā of the city of the triad is the fourth seat, which is distinct [from the others].

The Mother is the Goddess who has entered into the space [of consciousness]; the means for the realization of that is the valid cognition (*māna*); and the object of knowledge (*meyam*), when being known, is Mahātripurasundarī herself. Thus, having experienced the state of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge, She sports. Furthermore, there are the three abodes (*dhāmatraya*) beginning with Vāgbhava, the three sacred seats (*pīṭhatraya*) beginning with Kāmagiri, and the three powers (*śaktitraya*) beginning with Will (*icchā*).

Thus, through these various distinctions, because they consist of the *bindu*, the three genders— beginning with the *svāyaṃbhuva*— which are differentiated within those various abodes (*dhāma*) and so forth in their sequential order,
are indeed distinguished by the differentiation of the letter *a* within the triad of *mātṛkās*; this is due to the filling out of all such things in this manner.
He states that the supreme power (parā-śakti) named Tripurā has manifested as the collective totality (tatsamaṣṭi) of those [three] with the words "thus, she whose cities are the triad.

Thus, in the manner previously described, she is one whose constituent parts (tritayāni) are the cities (purāṇi), that is, bodies; for this very reason, she is the seat (pīṭha) of the fourth state (turīya), meaning she is the ground for the manifestation and withdrawal of the entire phenomenal world (sarvaprapañca) which consists of these threefold aspects.

From this point onward, by means of describing the qualities residing in the elements of the first created manifestation— namely ether, air, fire, water, and earth— as they arise from color, he begins to explain the nature of the deity consisting of the great mantra characterized by specific syllable counts.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are the subtle elements (bhūtasūkṣma).
The first is pervasive and each subsequent one is pervaded; thus, in sequence, there are fifteen [qualities]. 15.
This Nityā, consisting of fifteen syllables, is indeed considered to be composed of the elements;
likewise, the eternal qualities such as sound and the rest, which are divided into various distinctions, are pervaded by her. (16)
The lunar days (tithis), which are eternal and take the form of the lunar phases, possess the nature of the union of Śiva and Śakti;
they consist of day and night, and those venerable phonemes (varṇas) likewise embody that duality. (17)

Sound is the quality of space, touch is the quality of air, form is the quality of fire, taste is the quality of water, and smell is the quality of earth. Beginning with space and extending up to earth, these qualities increase one by one in each subsequent element, resulting in fifteen qualities in total. Of these qualities:

By virtue of its fifteen-fold nature, the Śrīvidyā becomes fifteen-syllabled. It is considered "elemental" (bhautika) because it is desired and accepted as being related to the elements; therefore, having the form of fifteen syllables—since the qualities of the primordial elements are fifteen—the syllables of the Vidyā are also fifteen, and she is of that very form.

She is of that very nature: eternal and immutable, she is the ground for the manifestation of all things, just as the ocean is the source of waves, bubbles, and foam. She is the sixteenfold [Śodhāśī] herself, who is established within the fifteen lunar days (tithis) consisting of fifteen parts.

He describes the nature of the fifteen-syllable mantra as consisting of the fifteen deities: "The Nityās have the form of the lunar days. The Nityās are those beginning with Kāmeśvarī and ending with Viśrāntā. Having the form of the lunar days means they are the deities who preside over the lunar days (*tithi*). And the lunar days, beginning with the first day (*pratipad*) and ending with the full moon, possess the form of the union of Śiva and Śakti.
They have the form of the union of *prakāśa* (light) and *vimarśa* (reflective awareness). For this very reason, they consist of day and night;

since light and reflective awareness consist of day and night, those lunar days (*tithis*) are the venerable phonemes (*śrīvarṇāḥ*). Those venerable phonemes, moreover, take fifteen forms by that aforementioned nature, and they also possess the qualities of the phonemes contained within the Vidyā.

The meaning is that they possess a dual form, consisting of such light (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). Herein lies the distinction: this very supreme power (*parā śakti*), composed of light and reflective awareness, consists of the five elements through the process of successive increase.
She has become the embodiment of the deities presiding over the fifteen lunar days (*tithi*), which correspond to the number of measures (*mātrā*) and syllables (*akṣara*).
According to the scripture:
"The Supreme Maheśvara is one alone, known as Light (*prakāśa*)."
The power of that [consciousness], called *vimarśa*, is proclaimed by the wise to be eternal.
And that Goddess, known as Vimarśa, has attained a fivefold state through the division of ether,
air, fire, water, and earth.
By the progressive increase of each individual quality, she has attained the number of lunar days (fifteen).
That Vidyā, which is proclaimed as the sixteenth and whose nature is reflective awareness (vimarśa),
is the Supreme Goddess Tripurā, who has manifested through sixteen divisions.
The [mandala] beginning with Sundarī and ending with Vicitrā, extending everywhere,
is to be understood from one's own scripture (svāgama) alone, by means of mere mental resolve.
Thus [ends the section]. 15 || 16 || 17 ||
In order to further solidify the very point already stated, he speaks in order to describe how knowledge (vidyā), like the deity, possesses both a universal nature and a state of transcendence:
"Its form is manifested through the divisions of the vowels, consonants, the three points (bindus), and their collective union."
Vidyā consists of the thirty-six principles and, transcending the principles, she is the absolute (kevalā). || 18 ||
The Vidyā, too, is of such a nature—that subtle Goddess Tripurasundarī;
the Noble Ones maintain the absolute non-difference between the Vidyā and that which is to be known by the Vidyā. (19)
The vowels are the *ac* letters, and the consonants are the *hal* letters. The three dots (*bindu*) are the three *anusvāras*.

Their "totality" (*samaṣṭi*) is their collective state, while their "differentiation" (*bheda*) is their individual constituent state. Her form is manifested by these; that is, her essential nature is revealed through them.
For this very reason, she is the essence of the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*), possessing a body extending from Śiva down to the earth (*kṣiti*), and yet she transcends all principles.

Because it is the locus for the assembly of the collection of principles (*tattva-saṃgha*), it transcends them; for this very reason, it is *kevalā* (solitary), being alone due to the absence of anything distinct from itself. Such is the *vidyā*, meaning the venerable fifteen-syllabled mantra (*śrī-pañcadaśākṣarī*). This is the method of dividing the constituent parts within this *vidyā*: here, in the *hādi-vidyā*, [the syllables] are Puṇya and Ānanda.

Those who possess extreme pride rely upon the collective totality of the constituent parts of this very Vidyā and declare it to be both identical with the principles (tattva) and transcendent of them. In that regard, within the first section called Vāgbhava, there are twelve phonemes formed by combining five vowels and seven consonants. [In] the one called Kāmarāja...
In the second section (*khaṇḍa*), there are six vowels and eight consonants, totaling fourteen phonemes (*varṇas*).

In the third section, called *Śakti*, there are four vowels and six consonants, totaling ten phonemes. Altogether, all these constitute thirty-six syllables, which exist both as constituent parts and as a collective whole.

Vidyā transcends all principles (tattvas) and is renowned everywhere; it is heard that even for a Vidyā beginning with *ka*, there exists indeed a dual nature (*ubhayātmakatva*), by which there is no difference between these two Vidyās. In the first section (*prathamakhaṇḍa*) beginning with *ha*, having combined the five vowels and seven consonants, [they appear] in both Vidyās in the first section.

Since the state of having twelve syllables is common [to both], both Vidyās indeed possess a dual nature. However, the method of practicing these two Vidyās must be understood from the mouth of the Guru alone. Furthermore, because the deity also possesses a dual nature just like the mantra, he states that there is an identity between the mantra and the deity: "The Vidyā also has such a nature."

Vidyā is of the nature of consciousness and bliss, consisting of that very essence, yet transcending it; she is subtle and impossible to fully delimit. She is renowned in all the Vedāntas as Tripurasundarī—both "Tripurā" and "Sundarī"—because she fulfills (pūraṇa) all things existing in the three cities (tripura), and because she is desirable as the object of worship for all yogis.

The etymology of the word *Tripurā* has already been explained in detail. The meaning is that the Goddess, whose nature is pure luminosity and who consists of the creative acts of generating the universe and so forth, is *Parā Vāk*; and all yogins, headed by the Supreme Lord, declare the absolute non-difference between her and the Self, which is both knowledge (*vidyā*) and the object of knowledge (*vedya*). || 19 ||

Having thus stated the non-difference between the Vidyā and the deity, he describes the manner in which the Cakra arises in order to express the identity between the Cakra and the deity: "That very same Great Goddess Parā, who consists of the form of the inner *oḥ*, is meditated upon as threefold."
Manifest as the essence of the three mothers beginning with Paśyantī, she attains the state of the wheel.
Even for the Wheel and the Great Goddess, not even a trace of difference is perceived by the wise;
between these two, though they appear gross, there is no distinction whatsoever, for their subtle form is the Supreme alone. (21)

Regarding the phrase "that whose form is accompanied by *antara-ūha*": *antara* refers to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), and *ūha* refers to deliberation (*vitarka*)—a state devoid of definitive determination such as "it is thus. She is that whose form is accompanied by that [deliberation]. The meaning is this:
because she is beyond the sphere of speech and mind, she cannot be delimited by any of the Vedāntas and is the cause of all things.

The Great Goddess (Maheśvarī) is said to be supreme (parā) and most excellent, as she is the ground for the manifestation of the entire collection of principles (tattvas) beginning with Śiva and ending with Earth.
And the Veda declares:
"His supreme power is heard to be indeed manifold; knowledge, strength, and action are His innate nature."

That very Supreme Power (*parā-śakti*), whose characteristic is such, is "conceived as threefold" (*tribhāvitā*), meaning she is perceived through a threefold mode. This is precisely what is stated [in the verse]: "clear, consisting of the three Mothers beginning with Paśyantī.

She is called "clear" (*spaṣṭā*) because she is intended as having arisen first; she is the subject who perceives, and thus she is called "Paśyantī. By the word "beginning" (*ādi*), [the other two are implied].

That very [power] is the Madhyamā and the Vaikharī; indeed, that which is called Vaikharī consists of the form of expression, comprises a collection of fifteen syllables, and is said to be the power (*śakti*) whose nature is all Vedic and worldly words. And so it is stated in the *Subhagodayavāsanā*:
Victorious is she who, as *parā*, perceives her birth arising from the clusters of creepers; as *madhyamā*, she is the fragrance; and as *vaikharī*, she is the rosary of syllables.

The meaning is that this very [deity], consisting of the three Mothers (trimātṛkā) of such a form, has attained the state of being the wheel (*cakratā*), as if having reached the unity of the wheel composed of the three sections (*trikhaṇḍā*). He says this very thing with the words "of the wheel" (*cakrasya*):
of the wheel consisting of nine enclosures (*āvaraṇa*) beginning with Trailokyamohana and ending with Vaindava, which serves as the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) for Sundarī.

Even the slightest difference, or even a slight distinction, between Maheśī—the presiding deity—and Sundarī is not conceived of, nor perceived, by the wise devotees of Maheśvara. Why? Because the Śrīcakra is of the very nature of Śrī Sundarī. Furthermore, he describes their such non-difference as follows: "The subtle form of these two..."
By such statements as these, it is shown that the "subtle nature" (*sūkṣmarūpatva*) of these two— the wheel (*cakra*) and the deity—
is simply their being unlimited (*aparicchinnatva*). In this regard, the abiding of the Śrīcakra in its subtle form as the *bindu*,
and the unlimitedness of that *bindu* within the supreme space of the *bindu* (*vaidava paramākāśa*), has already been elaborated upon.
It has already been stated [in the scripture] that the deity’s knowledge (*vidyā*) is likewise of such a nature, and so forth. Similarly,
regarding the grossness of both the wheel (*cakra*) and the deity, "grossness" here refers to the expansion of the wheel from the triangle up to the square, and of the deity as well.

The meaning is that there is no distinction (*bheda*) or difference between these two types of wheel-deities (*cakradevatā*), because they are both essentially the contemplation (*manana*) of Tripurā in the form of the various powers (*śakti*) beginning with Tripurāmbikā. He states the reason for this: "She herself is the subtle form.
That aforementioned Supreme Power (*para-ādiśakti*) alone is the subtle form; her form has become subtle.
The meaning is that these two possess their own intrinsic nature (svarūpa). || 20 || 21 ||

Beyond this, in order to describe the Śrīcakra— which consists of nine triangles (*navayoni*) and is the manifestation of the powers (*śakti*) beginning with Parā and Paśyantī— of the wheel that is the form of the deity, [the author] first states that the *Vaindava* wheel, known as *Sarvānandamaya*,
consists of the power Parā.
The center of the wheel should be the supreme state; this is indeed the principle of the Bindu (the Point).
And when that [Bindu] becomes swollen, it clearly transforms into the form of a triangle.
This is the cause of the triad beginning with Paśyantī, and it consists of the three seed-syllables (*bīja*).

It is the central point (*bindu-tattva*) arising in the center of the wheel consisting of the nine wombs (*navayoni*), whose nature as *bindu* has already been explained. This, when directly realized by oneself, is indeed the Supreme (*parā*) alone.

The meaning is that it is indeed the very nature of the Supreme Power (*parāśakti*). He states that when this very *bindu*-principle attains a state of expansion, then the triangle-wheel (*trikoṇacakra*) arises: "And when that becomes swollen. This means at whatever time, by the power of the unseen destiny (*adṛṣṭa*) of living beings, even that *bindu* becomes swollen—that is, it undergoes expansion.

The meaning is that it then becomes triangular in form, having transformed into the nature of the union of the Absolute Bliss (*anuttarānanda*) and Will (*icchā*). This triangle-wheel is the source of the triad beginning with Paśyantī;
the meaning is that it is the cause for the arising of the three powers headed by Paśyantī, Madhyamā, and Vaikharī. Thus it is said:
Likewise, the power of will (icchā-śakti) is Vāmā, abiding in the form of Paśyantī;
and the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti) is Jyeṣṭhā, proclaimed as the speech of Madhyamā.
Consisting of straight lines, she is established in the universe with a manifest form;
yet, during the state of worldly manifestation, she assumes the form of the Bindu.
Then, through the process of return, she becomes brilliantly radiant in the form of the Śṛṅgāṭa.
This power of action, however, is Raudrī, who is Vaikharī and whose form is the universe.
Thus: "and having the form of three seed-syllables" means that which has the form of the three seed-syllables—the Vāgbhava, Kāmarāja, and Śakti—which consist of three parts (trikhaṇḍa). || 22 ||
Then, within the venerable Bhaṭṭārikā herself, the principle of the Bindu (bindutattva) became the Śrīcakra, consisting of nine yonis facing upwards and downwards; thus he says:
"Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Ambikā, and Anuttarā are the constituent parts. (23)
These—will, knowledge, action, and the quiescent—are likewise the subsequent components;
this pair of syllables, both separate and combined, constitutes the elevenfold Paśyantī.

Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Ambikā, and by the word "and" (ca), Parāśakti—these five powers are portions of the Absolute (Anuttara). The meaning is that they have become, or arisen as, portions of the Absolute by virtue of being the downward-facing five triangles situated within the Śrīcakra. These four are Icchā, Jñāna, Kriyā, and Śāntā.
The powers (*śaktayaḥ*) are the upper limbs, consisting of four upward-facing triangles. The intended meaning is as follows:

these—Raudrī, Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Ambikā, as well as Icchā, Jñānā, Kriyā, and Śāntā—are both the manifestations of Parā and the upper limbs; thus, the nine-triangle [figure] consists of this group of nine powers.

Regarding the word "cakra": those two syllables, both separately and together—the separate being the individual form (*vyaṣṭi*) and the combined being the universal form (*samaṣṭi*)—are the two syllables well-known in all the Upaniṣads. By means of the logic of the "tongs" (*saṃdaṃśanyāya*), they constitute the full *ahaṃtā* (I-consciousness) whose nature is the light and reflection (*prakāśa-vimarśa*) consisting of the mantra composed of all phonemes.

The meaning is that those two syllables, when investigated by the intellect as having elevenfold nature, become elevenfold. From Parā to Śāntā, there is a group of ten powers; they constitute the individual form (*vyaṣṭi*), and because they also constitute the universal totality (*sarvasamaṣṭi*), they are one—thus, [the two syllables] are elevenfold in nature.
This very reality of the Bindu is the cause of Paśyantī. || 23 || 24 ||
From here on, in order to describe the manner of constructing the emanation-cakras (sṛṣṭicakra) consisting of eight, ten, and other spokes,

he concludes the sequence of the primary subject, the triangle-cakra (trikoṇacakra), with the following: "Thus, she whose self is the Kāmakalā consists of the nature of the three points (bindu) and the phonemes (varṇa)."
This Mother, whose nature consists of the three qualities, has assumed the form of a triangle. || 25 ||
One is the other...
Thus, in the manner previously described, Kāma is the essence of the *kāmakalā*, whose nature is pure luminosity and whose essence is the supreme syllable; he is Paramaśiva, while *kalā* is...

I am the supreme syllable whose form is the entirety of speech, and my very body is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). Thus, being of the nature of both [Śiva and Śakti] means possessing an innate and perfect sense of "I-ness" (*ahambhāva*). This has indeed been clearly stated in the passage: "The *bindu* is of the nature of the *ahaṃkāra*. Of such a form, she is the essence of the *Kāmakalā*, consisting of the phonemes that are the nature of the three *bindus*.
The *bindus* consist of the previously mentioned mixture of blood and semen;
their state is their *tattva*, and those phonemes such as the *vāgbhava* which possess that very nature are of that essence. Thus, it is said in the *Rahasyāmnāya*:
Know that one's own beautiful *śṛṅgāṭa* consists of three drops—
mixed, white, and red— and is ancient, having the nature of the *praṇava*.
The three lines are to be understood as pure consciousness, whose essence is Śiva;
this very [consciousness], having assumed the form of a triangle, is the ultimate reality consisting of the dense essence of conscious bliss,
and is the core of all scriptural traditions.
She is perceived as the Self through direct realization by the great masters of yoga who possess the cultivation of the universal "I-consciousness" (*viśvāhaṃbhāva*);
she consists of the three qualities and the powers of will, knowledge, and action; thus, for this very reason, she is one and the sole creator of the entire universe. And so says the scripture:
When the consciousness of supreme bliss is joined with the power of will,
they call that the triangle, beautiful with the fragrance of emission.
Thus [ends the section]. || 25 ||
Beyond this, he states that even Paśyantī, whose nature is radiant manifestation, possesses a ninefold character as the essence of the wheel of nine sources (*navayonicakra*):
"The other [form] consists of the creation of the individual manifestations of Vāmā and the rest."
By that, the ninefold self was born; the mother... ||

Distinct from that [Parā], there is Paśyantī, who consists of the manifestation of the individual emanations beginning with Vāmā; she is composed of the nine powers beginning with Vāmā and ending with Śāntā. For that reason, she is the Mother named Paśyantī, the progenitress, whose nature is the ninefold womb (*navayonicakra*), which is the cause for the manifestation of the collection of powers beginning with Vāmā and ending with Śāntā, consisting of the ninefold self.

"Born" means manifested. Here, something is said by way of reference to the powers (śaktis) such as Vāmā and the rest: therein, the one named Vāmā is called the "mother of the universe" because she vomits forth the manifold world situated within the triangle (śṛṅgāṭa).
Jyeṣṭhā is the performer of all auspiciousness; Raudrī is the dispeller of all diseases and the bestower of all desired things.
According to the position of the Pratyabhijñā, she is Śakti, Ambikā, Sphurattā, and Mahāsattā— the supreme Speech (parāvāk) that transcends all.

The powers of will, knowledge, and action—which are adept at beholding the manifestation of one's own self whose essential nature is fully perfected—exist in the forms of Paśyantī, Madhyamā, and Vaikharī; however, the fourth is Śāntā, as stated in the *Catuḥśatī* and according to such Vedic revelation as, "Śāntā is partless and tranquil. || 26 ||
Immediately thereafter, he states that the middle [channel] also possesses a ninefold nature by means of another method, through the two names designated as "the middle. (26)
That middle [power] is twofold, abiding in subtle and gross forms;
the subtle consists of the nine *nādas*, while the gross consists of the nine phonemes known as the *bhūtalipi*.

Since one of these two is the cause and the other is the effect, for that reason, this [effect] is indeed that [cause]; there is no difference between them, for identity is what is intended by the relationship of cause and effect. (28)

The Madhyamā [power] exists in a state of equilibrium between the Parā and Paśyantī; by its two designations—that is, its two names—it is therefore easily perceived by supreme yogins as the power named Madhyamā. It is of two kinds, of two types, due to its gross and subtle states; therein, the subtle one is experienced through the power of meditative absorption (samādhi).

The gross form (*sthūlākṛti*) is that which is always present, situated as a sequence of phonemes (*varṇāvalī*), and capable of being expressed by scholars, commoners, and others. He explains this very point [in the verse]: "The subtle consists of the nine sounds (*navanāda*); the gross consists of the nine phonemes (*navavarṇa*).
The meaning is this: from the abode of Mitra and Varuṇa, through the restraint of the vital breath (*vāyu*).

That Kuṇḍalinī who is experienced as consisting of manifold *nādas*, which, preceded by the piercing of the lotuses beginning with Svādhiṣṭhāna, approaches the lap of Paramaśiva seated upon the lotus-throne at the end of the twelve (*dvādaśānta*), is the Great Mother (*mahāmātṛkā*).
The Great Maheśvaras, who have attained all goals through meditative absorption, regard her as their own self.

She consists of nine sounds: the first is *ciṇī*, the second is *ciṇiciṇī*, the third is the sound of a bell (*ghaṇṭānāda*), the fourth is the sound of a conch (*śaṅkhanāda*), the fifth is the sound of a lute string (*tantrīnāda*), the sixth is the sound of cymbals (*tālanāda*), and the seventh is... [the eighth is the sound of a flute (*veṇunāda*) and the ninth is the sound of a drum (*murajannāda*)].

The sound of the flute is the eighth, the sound of the kettledrum is the ninth, and the sound of the mṛdaṅga drum is [the tenth]. Regarding the term *bhūtalipi*, "bhūta" means elements and "lipi" means scripts; thus, *bhūtalipayaḥ* refers to those scripts which are elemental. Here, the "elemental nature" (*bhūtatva*) of the scripts consists in their being manifested by the placement of letters through specific gestures; however, that [nature] is merely a conceptual construction (*kalpanāmātra*) regarding the letters.

Because they consist of the power whose nature is the form of light (*tejorūpaśakti*), their name—that is, their designation—is [the same]. For the subtle *madhyamā* has indeed become the causal state of the gross one; since she is one and the same, he says "the first is the cause," and so forth.
"The first" refers to the previously mentioned subtle one, who is the cause because she arises first; "the other" refers to the gross one.

Because it is produced from that, there is therefore a relationship of cause and effect between these two, the subtle and the gross; for that reason, by that cause, this gross [form] is indeed that same subtle power—there is no difference, for there is truly no distinction. Now, one might ask: how can there be a relationship of cause and effect in the absence of difference?

To this, he replies: "Identity" (*tādātmya*). Identity consists of both difference and non-difference; it is intended as the relationship between cause and effect, or producer and produced, as in the case of clay and a jar. Because it is merely a matter of verbal designation (*vācārambhaṇamātra*), a single reality itself becomes twofold.
The meaning is that it is agreed upon by all the Vedāntas. || 27 || 28 ||

Immediately thereafter, he describes the manifestation of the power of Vaikharī by means of defining the eight-spoked wheel (*aṣṭakoṇa*) and other wheels, which consist of the radiation of light from the central hexagon (*madhya-ṣṛṅgāṭa*):
"That eight-spoked [wheel] consists of the *śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, and *pa* groups; it is the expansion of the central corner."
The nine corners and the center—within this group of ten, which is the lamp of the lamp of consciousness.
Consisting of the *śa-ṣa-sa* and *pa*-class phonemes— that is, having the eight corners of the [lotus] whose nature consists of the *śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, and *pa* classes as its expansion—

[the goddess] has withdrawn that nine-cornered [figure] together with its central triangle, as well as the center called the *bindu*, into this ten-fold [wheel] which is the lamp of the lamp of consciousness for the triangle, the eight-cornered [figure], and the rest.

The meaning is: [she is] Tripurā, who has become light, mounted upon the *bindu*-cakra according to the manner described as "the mass of consciousness-fire of the *saṃvarta* [dissolution] rooted in the *baindava-āsana*," and illuminated by a mass of radiance. || 29 ||
This pair of shadows is extended as two ten-spoked wheels;

that is to say, the pair of shadows— the double radiance— of the previously mentioned triad of wheels consisting of a mass of light has transformed into the nature of the two wheels named "Accomplisher of All Aims" and "Bestower of All Protection."
And so it has been said:
"The ten-spoked [wheel] whose form is a radiance throbbing with nine triangles."
He explains the essential nature of those two wheels:
"The expansion of its corners is made distinct by the flashing of the four groups beginning with *ta*, *ṭa*, *ca*, and *ka*. (30)

The inner ten-spoked wheel consists of the ten syllables comprising the *tavarga* and *ṭavarga*; the outer ten-spoked wheel consists of the ten spokes comprising the syllables of the *cavarga* and *kavarga*—this is the meaning. || 30 ||

Endowed with the radiance of this group of four, it is the transformation of the ten-spoked [wheel]. This means that the "transformation of the ten-spoked" refers to the external ten-spoked wheel, which is endowed with— that is, joined with— the splendor or luster of this group of four wheels consisting of the Bindu, the Triangle, the Octagon, and the inner Ten-spoked [wheel].
The meaning is that, precisely because of the proximity of the four wheels beginning with the *baindava* to the outer ten-spoked wheel (*bahirdaśāracakra*), its respective radiance pervades them;
and so it has been stated:
"Through the transformation associated with the form of light from the four wheels.
Thus [it is said].
Now, he describes the nature of this fourfold wheel, which consists of a triangle, an eight-spoked figure, and two ten-spoked figures:
"The fourteen-spoked [wheel] arose, consisting of the fourteen letters beginning with the first vowel. (31)
The meaning is that this is the wheel named "Bestower of All Prosperity" (Sarvasaubhāgyadāyaka), which consists of fourteen syllables beginning with 'a' and is endowed with fourteen corners. || 31 ||
Thus, he states that the power of Vaikharī has manifested through the description of the wheels (cakras) beginning with the Bindu and ending with the corners of the mantra:
"By means of Parā, Paśyantī, and also Madhyamā, which consists of gross phonemes."
By these [syllables], Vaikharī, consisting of forty-nine syllables, was produced. || 32 ||

The meaning is this: Vaikharī is that which consists of the entire collection of phonemes from 'a' to 'kṣa', the creator of the whole phenomenal world, and whose essence is all speech-sounds. || 32 ||

Henceforth, he states that the two wheels named Sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇa and Sarvāśāparipūraka consist precisely of the phonemes of the *vaikharī* [speech]: "The eight-petaled lotus is augmented by the eight letters beginning with *ka*, and by the groups of *vaikharī* sounds."
And this lotus of sixteen petals should be visualized as arising from the assembly of the musical scales (svaragaṇa). || 33 ||

The wheel that thoroughly agitates all (Sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇacakra) is an eight-petalled lotus, perfectly interwoven and augmented by the eight groups of *vaikharī*— the nature of which is the *vaikharī* power— beginning with the letter *ka*. Likewise, this visible [wheel] is fully permeated and arisen from the collection of vowels, being properly cultivated by the sixteen phonemes beginning with the vowel *a*.
The meaning is that one should always meditate upon the lotus of sixteen petals, which is the wheel that fulfills all aspirations. || 33 ||
These circles consist of the threefold light composed of the three *bindus* and the transformation of the triad;
this is the triad of earth-mandalas, the resting place of the three Mothers beginning with Paśyantī.
Those *vṛtta*s (circles) are situated upon the *manvaśra* (octagon), upon an eight-petalled lotus, and upon a sixteen-petalled lotus.

They consist of the triad of drops (*bindu*) previously mentioned—composed of red, white, and mixed—which are themselves modifications of that triad of energies consisting of the moon, sun, and fire; this is the meaning of "consisting of that" (*tanmaya*). In that regard:

By the statement that the three circles consist of the three fires (tejas), it is indicated that the wheel is composed of the three segments of the Moon, Sun, and Fire; and the phrase "their modification" should be understood in the same way as the Vedic principle: "the Vedas are the authority.
The three earth-disks (bhūbimba) [represent] the powers beginning with *aṇimā* and the goddesses beginning with Brāhmī.

The meaning is that the collection of powers beginning with the *sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī* mudrā, which constitute the latent impressions (*vāsanā*), find rest in the three Mothers beginning with *paśyantī*; these powers— *paśyantī*, *madhyamā*, and *vaikharī*— expanding up to this point, shine forth as the essence of the Śrīcakra, extending from the triangle (*trikoṇa*) to the outer square (*bhūpura*).
And this has been thoroughly explained by the web of texts beginning with "This is the manifestation of the Self" and ending with "Vaikharī has the universe as her form. || 34 ||

Having thus correctly described the Śrīcakra of the venerable Mahātripurasundarī, beginning with "Thus the center of the wheel would be" and ending with "resting in the three Mothers, Paśyantī and the rest," he subsequently [described] her [powers], ending with "the supernatural powers such as aṇimā and so forth."

He states that even the assembly of powers (*śakti-nikuramba*) contained within the wheel of obstructions (*āvaraṇa-cakra*), as well as the circle of the venerable Gurus situated near it, are indeed nothing but the transformation of the limbs of the venerable Goddess:
"The 'krama' is the stepping of the feet; by that, the 'arising of the krama' (*kramodaya*) is said to be twofold."
This pair of guru lineages is the unfolding of the lotus feet of the Mother. 35.

*Kramaṇa* is the sequential movement of the *pada*; it is of two kinds: that consisting of the projection of the *pada* (*padavikṣepa*) and that consisting of the emergence of the sequence (*kramodaya*). Among these, *padavikṣepa* is the capacity to generate infinite powers consisting of infinite millions of rays for the sake of the beautiful ones (*sundarī*). *Kramodaya*, on the other hand, is...

The expansion occurs by way of being identical with the Śrī-guru-maṇḍala, whose nature is infinite light consisting of the streams of divine, perfected, and human [beings]. He explains this pair of circles as the "enclosure" (*āvaraṇa*); that is, the multitude of powers situated within the enclosure-circle, according to the maxim "the platforms are shouting. [This refers to] the lineage of gurus (*gurupaṅkti*).

This twofold mandala of the Guru is the expansion of the lotus feet of Ambā; that is to say, it is the expansion, the spreading forth, the manifestation of the lotus feet—the pair of glorious feet—of Ambā Tripurā. || 35 ||
This very Supreme Maheśī, who gradually unfolds the expansion of that [power], when she transforms herself into the form of a wheel (cakra),
then the transformation of the limbs of her body becomes all the deities of the enclosures (āvaraṇadevatās). || 36 ||
Seated upon the wheel consisting of the *bindu*, that Goddess Tripurasundarī resides on the lap of Kāmeśvara, her crest-jewel fashioned from a digit of the moon.
Her own hands are adorned with a noose, a goad, a sugarcane bow, and five flower-arrows;
her limbs are as red as the rising sun, and she possesses three eyes in the form of the moon, the sun, and fire.

This very [deity] consists of an undivided mass of infinite splendor; she is the supreme, most excellent [power], whose nature is eternal and limitless, unsurpassed bliss worshipped by the multitude of infinite crores of Yoginīs.
This ninefold wheel, consisting of nine distinct mantras, is as follows:
Thus, one should perceive the radiance of one's own self as consisting of the nine cakras, beginning with the Baindava and ending with the Trailokyamohana;
at the moment of beholding the self composed of perfect bliss, one should transform into another form.

Regarding the limbs of her body: the body of that Tripurā consists of a mass of light, and likewise, her limbs are rays; their transformation is the attainment of a different state. Here, the deities of the enclosures (āvaraṇadevatās)—the multitude of infinite powers such as Vaśinī, Aṇimā, and so forth—are indeed of the nature of an ocean of consciousness and bliss.

The meaning is that, within the state of proximity, infinite millions of powers undergo manifestation and withdrawal, like foam, bubbles, waves, and so forth. "Seated," etc., refers to the supreme space called Sarvānanda, which consists of the *bindu*.

The meaning is that, because it has been stated [in the scripture] "in the *bindu*, in the supreme space" (*bindave paramākāśe*), she— Tripurasundarī, who is of that very nature and is unconditioned by place, time, or form— is seated upon the wheel (*cakra*), the sacred seat (*pīṭha*) for the movement and abiding of the Self, shining resplendently in the upper region.

She is desirable as the cause of all things, or she is pure; she is one whose abode is the lap of Kāmeśvara—that is, the lap is the beautiful part of his thigh, and her abode is that place of residence. Thus it has been said by Paramaśiva:
Kalā, Vidyā, and Parāśakti take the form of the Śrīcakra;
in its center is the station of Bindu, where the Supreme Goddess resides.

"United with Sadāśiva, she contains within her the meaning of all the principles (*tattva*s)," and so forth. The Goddess finds delight in activities such as the creation of the universe. "Bond" (*pāśa*) refers to the binding of one's own self through differentiation; it is the nature of the power of will (*icchā-śakti*). "Goad" (*aṅkuśa*)...

Consisting of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), it has as its nature the means for shattering the differentiation of one's own essential form (*svarūpa-bheda*). Within the pentad of the sugarcane bow, the flower, and the arrows—which are the very nature of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) functioning as the instruments that assume forms non-different from Himself—the meaning is this: the powers of will (*icchā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and action (*kriyā*) themselves, having assumed the nature of the fetters (*pāśa*) and so forth by His command, perform their worship.
This is the meaning. And thus:
"Bearing the noose consisting of the power of will (icchā-śakti), the goad in the form of knowledge (jñāna), and the radiant bow and arrow consisting of the power of action (kriyā-śakti)."
Thus [ends the section]. || 36 || 37 || 38 ||
It is said that the divine siddhas worship this very divine couple, whose nature is the mandala of gurus distinguished by the non-distinction of differences:
"That couple resides within the triangle consisting of the three points, due to the differentiation of qualities."
It is expanded out as the nature of the three pairs, headed by Kāmeśvara and Mitreśvari. || 39 ||
That couple, transcending all things, is the form of Kāma and Kāmeśvarī, as is well known from all the Upaniṣads.
This is the meaning: the Supreme Self, having made its very own self consist of female and male, sports in the form of a couple;
it exists as a union consisting of Light (prakāśa) and Reflection (vimarśa).
It is Paramaśiva alone who has brought down the entire Tantra. And thus, that couple—in the form of Kāma and Kāmeśvarī; Mitreśvarī and Śrīmad-Ūrdhvadīpanātha; Vajreśvarī and Jyeṣṭhānātha;
Bhagamālinī and Mitradevanātha—exists as the essence of these three couples and so forth.
The meaning is that the triad of couples has spread out, expanded in the form of the sequence beginning with the divine, the perfected, and the human streams.

From here onwards, he describes the nature and manifestation of the deities of the enclosures: "Those who dwell in the eight-petaled lotus, beginning with Vaśinī, are as red as the twilight; this very subtle body (puryaṣṭaka) belongs to the Goddess, whose form is the wheel and whose essence is consciousness. (40)
The eight powers, beginning with Vaśinī, who dwell in the Vasukoṇa, whose nature it is to reside in the wheel known as Sarvarogahara (the Remover of All Diseases),

and who are capable of bestowing the bliss of the perfect state of "I-ness" (pūrṇāhaṃbhāva)— how can their quality of being "removers of disease" here be anything other than the very granting of that perfect state of "I-ness"?

As it is said: "The sense of being incomplete is a disease, the sole repository of wretchedness. Such are these [energies], which shine with the reddish hue of twilight (saṃdhyāruṇā), meaning they appear in the form of the dawn-red (aruṇākārā). For this very reason, this eight-cornered wheel belongs to her whose self (ātman) is consciousness (saṃvit); that is, she whose nature (svarūpa) is consciousness itself, which is knowledge (jñāna).
It is that which is "truth, knowledge, and infinite," according to the Vedic scripture.
"Tripurā the Goddess is self-consciousness...
and from such scriptural sources [we know] that the Goddess [thinks],
"May I be many, may I procreate."

Thus, the meaning is that the body of the Śrīcakra-tanu, which has the nature of movement and consists of the wheels [of the cakra], is the subtle body of the eightfold city (sūkṣmapuryaṣṭaka). || 40 ||

Those functions directed toward that object, having attained the very nature of the Omniscient One and others, shine within the abode of the inner ten spokes, beautiful in form like the autumnal moon. (41)
Their functional manifestations (vṛttis) reside near the eight corners;
they are renowned for maintaining the protection of the essential forms of the Vasus and others, have attained the nature of the ten powers such as omniscience,
dwell within the inner ten spokes, and are mounted upon the wheel designated as the "performer of all protection."
The Yoginīs of the Inner Essence (nigarbha), beautiful in form like the autumn moon and possessing a self-luminous white appearance, gleam and shine forth. || 41 ||
In the outer rows and corners of that [mandala], the Yoginīs who bestow all siddhis are situated in the east;
they consist of the goddesses, the intellect, the organs of action, and their objects, and are enriched with bright garments and ornaments. (42)

In the outer rows and corners of that wheel which provides all protection— located in the outer regions above the wheel that accomplishes all aims (sarvārthasādhaka)— reside the ten yoginīs known as Kulakaula, who grant all siddhis and are headed by Sarvasiddhi.

The *śaktis* consist of the goddesses whose nature is the objects of the sensory and motor organs; that is, they are identical in essence (*tanmayī*) with the sensory and motor organs of the goddess Tripurā and their respective objects, being of that very form. They are "rich in bright attire and ornaments" (*viśada-veśa-bhūṣā-ḍhyāḥ*), meaning they are radiant (*viśada*) and white in appearance, and are enriched by both their dress (*veśa*) and ornaments (*bhūṣā*). This is the meaning.
The meaning is that they appear with clear forms and white ornaments, bestowing the attainment of the nature of non-difference between the mantra, the deity, and the self. || 42 ||

The Yoginīs of the oral tradition are to be meditated upon as dwelling within the wheel of the city of the worlds, flashing forth through the expansion of imitative sounds, and clothed in garments the color of twilight.
The wheel of the array of worlds (*bhuvanāracakra*) is the wheel that bestows all prosperity; "abode" (*bhavana*) refers to their dwelling place.

Those [entities] which imitate the Goddess are the fourteen instruments (*karaṇa*): the five organs of knowledge (*jñānendriya*), the five organs of action (*karmendriya*), and the four known as mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), and consciousness (*citta*). This is their detailed exposition.
The meaning is that those goddesses possess a radiance (*sphuraṇa*) that serves as their explanation and takes the form of fourteen spokes;
the Goddess herself exists as the very essence of the deities of the fourteen-spoked wheel consisting of the fourteen instruments (*karaṇa*).
Those [goddesses] have garments (*vasana*) whose color is identical to—that is, similar to—that of the Twilight (*saṃdhyā*).

The Yoginīs of the Tradition, who consist of the primordial Śakti and are to be known through the true tradition, beginning with Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī and the others, should be meditated upon—that is, they should be properly contemplated. || 43 ||

Victorious are those known as the most secret Yoginīs, whose forms are the unmanifest, the Great Principle (mahat), the ego (ahaṃkāra), and the subtle elements (tanmātra) transformed into the shape of beloved women, abiding within the lotus that covers the elephant. 44.

The Unmanifest (avyakta), the principle called the Unmanifest; the Great Principle (mahattattva); the ego-sense (ahaṃkṛti), the principle of ego; and the subtle elements (tanmātrāḥ)—the five subtle elements of the gross elements beginning with earth—these eight, taken together, constitute those whose desired form or essential nature is composed of the Goddesses; this is the meaning.

Because they are the most intimate inner circle of the Goddess Bhūta, these [deities] beginning with Anaṅgakusumā are known by the name "most secret" (guptatara). They triumph—that is, they exist in a state of supreme excellence—within the eight-petaled lotus called Sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇa, which is the lotus that serves as the elephant’s skin. || 44 ||
The elements, the ten senses, and the mind constitute the sixteenfold transformation of the Goddess;
in her essential nature as Kāmākarṣiṇī and the others, she dwells in the center of the sixteen-spoked [cakra]. (45)

The elements, beginning with earth, the ten sense organs, and the mind— this sixteen-spoked wheel named "Fulfiller of All Desires"— He presides over and governs in the form of the sixteen powers (śaktis), such as Kāmākarṣiṇī and the rest, within this Fulfiller of All Desires.
The meaning is that these Guptayoginīs, beginning with Kāmākarṣaṇī, who are the essence of all things, reside within the wheel (cakra). || 45 ||
All the mudrās, together with the Trikhaṇḍā, consist of pure consciousness and are raised aloft;
they dwell within the primordial abode of the earth and resemble the radiance of the rising sun.
The nine supports, abiding as the nine wheels, have undergone transformation;
the nine Lords and their Śaktis likewise take the form of Mudrās.
Because they liberate from the floods of bonds such as the planetary influences and cause them to dissolve, they are proclaimed as Mudrās—liberation and dissolution being the reason for their name.
And she made them into wheels. || 47 ||

Together with the triple-sectioned [mudrā], that is, along with the mudrā known as *trikhaṇḍā*, they are fully uplifted—meaning they exist in a state of perfect elevation and supreme excellence. Their original abodes are on the earth, namely their square-shaped dwellings;
they are equal to the radiance of the rising sun, possessing a luster similar to the brilliance of the youthful dawn, and they consist of pure consciousness (*saṃvinmayī*).

The meaning is that they are established in the density of consciousness (*ciddhana*). These *mudrās*, moreover, have been elaborated upon by Paramaśiva as the presiding deities of the nine cakras, beginning with the square (*caturaśra*) and ending with the bindu (*vaindava*).
He explains this very point in the passage beginning with "ādhāra," etc.; the "ninefold foundation" (*ādhāranavaka*) refers to the Mūlādhāra, Svādhiṣṭhāna, and so forth.

The meaning is that for her, who is the form of the worshipper, the Maṇipūraka, Anāhata, Bhrūmadhya, Viśuddhi, Lambikā, Ājñā, and Bindu—belonging to her—are related to the nine cakras; by reason of which [cakras] having been transformed into the nature of the Bindu (baindava), the nine Śaktis of the Nāthas have become transformed into the form of the nine Mudrās. || 45 || 47 ||
Its sevenfold [sheaths] beginning with the skin, as well as its eightfold form, are clearly manifest;
this central orb of the earth occupies the forms of the Mothers, Brāhmī and the others. (48)

The meaning is that this Goddess dwells in the central square, bearing the eightfold form consisting of the seven constituents beginning with the skin (the seven dhātus such as skin, blood, etc. and her own essential nature (ākāra-svarūpa), which is the form of the Mothers beginning with Brāhmī—the essential nature of the eight powers beginning with Brāhmī. || 48 ||

The powers beginning with *aṇimā*, having assumed the forms of lovely women, exist as the fruits [of this vidyā] by way of being subordinate qualities to other vidyās, residing in the earthly abode. (49)
The eight powers of this Supreme Sovereign, beginning with *aṇimā*, possess the lovely and enchanting forms of beautiful women that have been adopted by other sciences such as Haṭhayoga;
being thus constituted, they abide within the square at the base of the earth (*bhūniketanagāḥ*) in a subordinate or secondary capacity.
This is the meaning. || 49 ||

From "hereafter the lineage of gurus is declared" up to the end of these four verses, the experience of supreme bliss— which is the essence of the *bindu* (the point) and non-different from the Supreme Guru— is set forth by means of the mantra of the lineage of gurus ending with Paramaśiva, out of a desire to favor the disciples.

Furthermore, that [consciousness], gradually becoming undifferentiated, attained the state of the Lord of Desire (Kāmeśvara), which is the nature of the self-reflection of consciousness (cidvimarśa). || 50 ||

The "Supreme" (parama) is the most excellent experience consisting of the fullness of the sense of "I" (paripūrṇāhaṃbhāva); He whose knowledge [is this] is the Supreme Guru, and so forth. From that Ādinātha, who is the Supreme Guru and Paramaśiva, the Bindu is non-distinct and inseparable; it is of the nature of the previously mentioned Kāmakalā, and He whose essential nature (svarūpa) is that [Bindu] is the Self (Ātman).
Seated upon the Śrīpīṭha in the Kṛtayuga age, Guru Śiva imparted the Vidyā to his consort Kāmeśvarī, who is the embodiment of reflective awareness (vimarśa).
She also [worshipped] her own portions, headed by Īśa and Mitreśa, known as Jyeṣṭha, Madhyama, and Māla;
and the three Gurus who are the causes of the Tretā and other ages, whose forms consist of consciousness, vital breath, and the objects of the senses.
Having examined the presiding deities of the three seed-syllables, he revealed the Vidyā;
thus has the lineage of gurus been declared in order to grace the three currents.
This play of the woman who is the digit of desire (Kāmakalā), arisen from the bliss of merit, is ever conducive for one whose mind is drawn by the serpent-noose of Supreme Śiva. 54.
Homage to that illustrious Lord, the navigator, by whose grace one has crossed the ocean of the manifold expansion of the waters of craving, which is the inner fickleness of the mind. 55.
Thus ends the *Kāmakalāvilāsa*, composed by the venerable ascetic Puṇyānanda.
When the assembly of texts and learned scholars— the refuge of the six sciences— had undergone decline due to the course of time,
[this work was composed] for the sake of professional activity by one endowed with the vigor of true discernment and single-mindedly intent on upholding those various True Dharmas.

Having deliberated with his chief ministers who were devoted to the Dharma, the illustrious sovereign of Kashmir established the primary office for the purpose of extracting the texts containing the essence of spiritual knowledge and realized wisdom.

May this work, which has been refined through completion, purification, and exposition by virtuous men who have entered upon the livelihood [of the Vaiṣṇavas] under the supervision of Mukunda Rāma, be for the welfare of the good.
(Tilaka)
May this be offered unto the glorious Śiva.
May there be auspiciousness for the practitioner, the reader, and the listener.
